title: Μενέλαος καὶ Εὔφορβος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Book 17 opens with the fight over the body of Patroclus. Menelaus strides round the fallen man like a mother over her first calf, and Euphorbus, who struck the first blow at Patroclus, orders him off and boasts that he will take the armour. Menelaus answers with a boast of his own, Euphorbus lunges and fails, and Menelaus kills him with a thrust through the neck. Apollo, in the likeness of Mentes, rouses Hector by telling him that the horses of Achilles cannot be caught and that Euphorbus is dead. Hector comes shouting through the front ranks, and Menelaus, who sees him, argues with himself: he cannot leave the armour and Patroclus, but he cannot face Hector alone, with a god behind him. He decides to go and look for Ajax.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔλαθ’ Ἀτρέος υἱὸν ἀρηΐφιλον Μενέλαον
Πάτροκλος Τρώεσσι δαμεὶς ἐν δηϊοτῆτι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ elath’ Atreos huion arēïphilon Menelaon
Patroklos Trōessi dameis en dēïotēti.
sentences.l:
Nor did he escape the notice of the son of Atreus, Ares-loved Menelaus,
Patroclus, subdued by the Trojans in the fighting.
sentences.i: Patroclus, overcome by the Trojans in the fighting, did not escape the notice of Menelaus, son of Atreus, dear to Ares.
sentences.n: Book 17 begins where Book 16 ended: Patroclus has just been killed, and the fight now turns on his body. The subject of ἔλαθ’ (λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’, which takes the accusative) is Patroclus, named only in line 2; the person who notices is Menelaus, in the accusative. Ἀτρέος υἱόν ‘son of Atreus’ and ἀρηΐφιλον ‘dear to Ares’ are stock phrases for Menelaus. δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue, overcome’ (‘tame’ is said of horses), and δηϊοτῆτι is the dative of δηϊοτής ‘fighting’.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῷ βαῖν’ ὥς τις περὶ πόρτακι μήτηρ
πρωτοτόκος κινυρὴ οὐ πρὶν εἰδυῖα τόκοιο·
ὣς περὶ Πατρόκλῳ βαῖνε ξανθὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.tr:
bē de dia promachōn kekorythmenos aithopi chalkōi,
amphi d’ ar’ autōi bain’ hōs tis peri portaki mētēr
prōtotokos kinyrē ou prin eiduia tokoio·
hōs peri Patroklōi baine xanthos Menelaos.
sentences.l:
And he went through the front-fighters, armed with the fire-faced bronze,
and around him he strode, like a mother round her calf,
first-bearing, wailing, not before knowing childbirth;
so round Patroclus strode fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.i: He went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire, and strode round him as a mother strides round her calf, a first-time mother, wailing, who had never known childbirth before; so fair-haired Menelaus strode round Patroclus.
sentences.n: Line 3 stands word for word at 5.681 and again at line 87 of this part, and its English is kept. In line 4 αὐτῷ ‘him’ is Patroclus, whom the simile’s calf stands for, and βαῖν’ is βαῖνε, imperfect of βαίνω ‘stride’, here ‘bestride, stand guard’ over a fallen man. πρωτοτόκος means bearing for the first time, so the mother has no other young; κινυρή is ‘wailing’, a low plaintive cry, on the usual explanation. τόκοιο is an epic genitive after εἰδυῖα (the perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’).

sentences.t:
πρόσθε δέ οἱ δόρυ τ’ ἔσχε καὶ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην,
τὸν κτάμεναι μεμαὼς ὅς τις τοῦ γ’ ἀντίος ἔλθοι.
sentences.tr:
prosthe de hoi dory t’ esche kai aspida pantos’ eïsēn,
ton ktamenai memaōs hos tis tou g’ antios elthoi.
sentences.l:
and before him held both spear and shield equal on every side,
eager to kill the man who against him might come.
sentences.i: He held his spear and his shield, equal on every side, in front of him, eager to kill whoever might come against him.
sentences.n: The subject is still Menelaus, and οἱ ‘him’ is Patroclus. Both lines stand elsewhere in the Iliad, with a lion where Menelaus now is, and their English is kept. ἔσχε is the aorist of ἔχω, here ‘held’ (to protect). πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ is the stock phrase for a round shield. In line 8, τὸν is the object of κτάμεναι, the epic infinitive ‘to kill’, and ὅς τις … ἔλθοι is an indefinite relative clause with the optative: ‘whoever might come’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα Πάνθου υἱὸς ἐϋμμελίης ἀμέλησε
Πατρόκλοιο πεσόντος ἀμύμονος· ἄγχι δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτοῦ
ἔστη, καὶ προσέειπεν ἀρηΐφιλον Μενέλαον·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara Panthou huios eÿmmeliēs amelēse
Patrokloio pesontos amymonos· anchi d’ ar’ autou
estē, kai proseeipen arēïphilon Menelaon·
sentences.l:
Nor then was Panthus’ son, of the good ash-spear, unmindful
of Patroclus fallen, the blameless; and near him
he took his stand, and addressed Ares-loved Menelaus:
sentences.i: Nor was Panthus’ son, of the good ash-spear, unmindful of the fall of blameless Patroclus; he took his stand close by him, and spoke to Menelaus, dear to Ares:
sentences.n: Panthus’ son is Euphorbus, who is not named until line 59. ἀμέλησε is the aorist of ἀμελέω ‘be careless of, take no heed of’, and takes the genitive Πατρόκλοιο πεσόντος ἀμύμονος, ‘Patroclus having fallen, the blameless’. ἐϋμμελίης ‘of the good ash-spear’ is the stock epithet for a spearman. ἄγχι δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτοῦ is ‘and near him’ (the ἄρα is only a connective). The colon introduces his speech, which begins in line 12.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς ὄρχαμε λαῶν
χάζεο, λεῖπε δὲ νεκρόν, ἔα δ’ ἔναρα βροτόεντα·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē Menelae diotrephes orchame laōn
chazeo, leipe de nekron, ea d’ enara brotoenta·
sentences.l:
“Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, leader of the people,
give ground, and leave the corpse, and let be the bloody spoils;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, leader of the people, give ground, leave the corpse, and let the bloody spoils be;
sentences.n: Euphorbus speaks, and his words are a command in three parts: χάζεο ‘give ground’ (imperative of χάζομαι), λεῖπε ‘leave’, and ἔα ‘let be’ (imperative of ἐάω). Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’; διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured’ and ὄρχαμε λαῶν ‘leader of the people’ are stock vocatives, here used with an edge, since Euphorbus means to take the dead man’s armour from him. ἔναρα βροτόεντα are the ‘bloody spoils’, the armour stripped from the dead.
sentences.mark: Euphorbus tells Menelaus to give way

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις πρότερος Τρώων κλειτῶν τ’ ἐπικούρων
Πάτροκλον βάλε δουρὶ κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην·
sentences.tr:
ou gar tis proteros Trōōn kleitōn t’ epikourōn
Patroklon bale douri kata kraterēn hysminēn·
sentences.l:
for no one earlier of the Trojans and the famous allies
struck Patroclus with a spear in the strong battle;
sentences.i: for none of the Trojans or their famous allies struck Patroclus with a spear earlier than I did, in the strong battle;
sentences.n: πρότερος is the comparative ‘earlier, before’, and the Greek leaves out ‘than I’, which the sense needs, since Euphorbus is claiming the first blow on Patroclus. κλειτῶν ἐπικούρων ‘famous allies’ are the troops who fight beside the Trojans without being Trojans. βάλε is the aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’, and δουρί the dative ‘with a spear’. κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην ‘in the strong battle’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
τώ με ἔα κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἐνὶ Τρώεσσιν ἀρέσθαι,
μή σε βάλω, ἀπὸ δὲ μελιηδέα θυμὸν ἕλωμαι.
sentences.tr:
tō me ea kleos esthlon eni Trōessin aresthai,
mē se balō, apo de meliēdea thymon helōmai.
sentences.l:
so let me win good glory among the Trojans,
lest I strike you, and take your honey-sweet spirit from you.”
sentences.i: So let me win good glory among the Trojans, lest I strike you and take your honey-sweet spirit away.”
sentences.n: τώ ‘so, therefore’ draws the conclusion of the argument: since the first blow was Euphorbus’s, he asks to be allowed the credit. ἔα με … ἀρέσθαι is ‘let me win’; ἀρέσθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win, gain’. μή σε βάλω is a clause of purpose after a command (‘lest I strike you’), with the subjunctive. ἀπὸ … ἕλωμαι is the verb ‘take away’ split in two (tmesis). μελιηδέα ‘honey-sweet’ is the stock epithet of the θυμός ‘spirit’ that leaves a man at death.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Him then, greatly vexed, addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: Then, greatly troubled, fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
sentences.n: This line is a speech-introduction that the Odyssey uses word for word, and its English is kept. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed’, a mood of annoyance, and ξανθός ‘fair-haired’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet. Menelaus’ answer to Euphorbus runs from line 19 to line 32.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ οὐ μὲν καλὸν ὑπέρβιον εὐχετάασθαι.
sentences.tr: Zeu pater ou men kalon hyperbion euchetaasthai.
sentences.l: “Father Zeus, it is not good, truly, to boast exceedingly.
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, it is not fine to boast exceedingly.
sentences.n: He begins by calling on Zeus, with the vocative Ζεῦ πάτερ ‘Father Zeus’, and then criticises Euphorbus’ boasting. ὑπέρβιον is the neuter accusative used as an adverb, ‘beyond force’, so ‘exceedingly’. εὐχετάασθαι is the epic infinitive of εὔχομαι in the sense ‘boast, declare aloud’ (not ‘pray’), lengthened for the metre. καλόν ‘fair, good’ here means ‘fitting’.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ οὖν παρδάλιος τόσσον μένος οὔτε λέοντος
οὔτε συὸς κάπρου ὀλοόφρονος, οὗ τε μέγιστος
θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι περὶ σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνει,
ὅσσον Πάνθου υἷες ἐϋμμελίαι φρονέουσιν.
sentences.tr:
out’ oun pardalios tosson menos oute leontos
oute syos kaprou oloophronos, hou te megistos
thymos eni stēthessi peri stheneï blemeainei,
hosson Panthou huies eÿmmeliai phroneousin.
sentences.l:
Neither the leopard’s so great might, nor the lion’s,
nor the baneful-minded boar’s, whose greatest
spirit in his chest exults greatly in its strength,
as much as Panthus’ sons, of the good ash-spear, are minded.
sentences.i: Neither the leopard’s might, nor the lion’s, nor that of the baneful-minded boar, whose spirit in his chest is greatest and exults greatly in its strength, is as great as the pride Panthus’ sons, of the good ash-spear, carry in their minds.
sentences.n: This is a comparison of beasts, and the ‘sons of Panthus’ are the family of Euphorbus, who has just spoken. The sentence turns on τόσσον … ὅσσον ‘so great … as’: the might of leopard, lion and boar is set against the pride of Panthus’ sons. ὀλοόφρονος ‘baneful-minded’ describes the boar. σθένεϊ is the dative of σθένος ‘strength’, and βλεμεαίνει is ‘exults’. φρονέουσιν ‘think, are minded’ has no object here, and the sense is the proud thinking called μέγα φρονέειν elsewhere.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ βίη Ὑπερήνορος ἱπποδάμοιο
ἧς ἥβης ἀπόνηθ’, ὅτε μ’ ὤνατο καί μ’ ὑπέμεινε
καί μ’ ἔφατ’ ἐν Δαναοῖσιν ἐλέγχιστον πολεμιστὴν
ἔμμεναι· οὐδέ ἕ φημι πόδεσσί γε οἷσι κιόντα
εὐφρῆναι ἄλοχόν τε φίλην κεδνούς τε τοκῆας.
sentences.tr:
oude men oude biē Hyperēnoros hippodamoio
hēs hēbēs aponēth’, hote m’ ōnato kai m’ hypemeine
kai m’ ephat’ en Danaoisin elenchiston polemistēn
emmenai· oude he phēmi podessi ge hoisi kionta
euphrēnai alochon te philēn kednous te tokēas.
sentences.l:
Nor even did the force of Hyperenor, horse-taming,
have profit of his own youth, when he made light of me and withstood me,
and called me among the Danaans the most shameful warrior
to be; nor do I say that on his own feet going
he gladdened his dear wife and his trusty parents.
sentences.i: Not even the force of Hyperenor, tamer of horses, had any benefit from his own youth, when he made light of me and withstood me and called me the most shameful warrior among the Danaans; and I do not say that, going on his own feet, he gladdened his dear wife and his trusty parents.
sentences.n: Hyperenor is a Trojan whom Menelaus killed in Book 14 (14.516–519); the Greek here does not say so. βίη Ὑπερήνορος is a periphrasis for the man himself: ‘the force of Hyperenor’. ἀπόνηθ’ is the aorist of ἀπονίναμαι ‘have profit of’ (the exact form is disputed), with the genitive ἧς ἥβης ‘his own youth’. ὤνατο is the aorist of ὄνομαι ‘make light of, find fault with’. ἐλέγχιστος ‘most shameful’ is a superlative, and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to be’. The last sentence means he did not return home alive; κιόντα ‘going’ is a participle that goes with ἕ ‘him’, the subject of the aorist infinitive εὐφρῆναι ‘gladdened’, all in indirect statement after φημί.

sentences.t:
ὥς θην καὶ σὸν ἐγὼ λύσω μένος εἴ κέ μευ ἄντα
στήῃς·
sentences.tr:
hōs thēn kai son egō lysō menos ei ke meu anta
stēēis·
sentences.l:
So surely I will loosen your might as well, if against me
you stand;
sentences.i: So I shall surely loosen your might as well, if you stand against me;
sentences.n: ὥς ‘so, in just that way’ points back to Hyperenor: Menelaus will do to Euphorbus what he did to him. θην is an emphatic ‘surely’. λύσω μένος is ‘loosen the might’, a phrase for killing: the limbs and strength of the dead man are ‘loosed’. εἴ κε … στήῃς is a future-open condition with the subjunctive of ἵστημι (aorist intransitive, ‘take your stand’), and μευ ἄντα is ‘face to face with me’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά σ’ ἔγωγ’ ἀναχωρήσαντα κελεύω
ἐς πληθὺν ἰέναι, μηδ’ ἀντίος ἵστασ’ ἐμεῖο
πρίν τι κακὸν παθέειν· ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω.
sentences.tr:
alla s’ egōg’ anachōrēsanta keleuō
es plēthyn ienai, mēd’ antios histas’ emeio
prin ti kakon patheein· rhechthen de te nēpios egnō.
sentences.l:
but I, for my part, bid you, stepping back,
to go into the crowd, and not to stand opposite me
before suffering some evil; a thing done a foolish one learns.”
sentences.i: But I, for my part, bid you step back into the crowd, and not stand to face me before you suffer some harm; even a foolish man learns when the thing is done.”
sentences.n: ἀναχωρήσαντα is the aorist participle of ἀναχωρέω ‘step back’, and ἰέναι ‘to go’ is the infinitive after κελεύω ‘bid’. Then the construction changes to a prohibition, μηδ’ … ἵστασ’ (= ἵστασο, present imperative middle ‘do not take your stand’), with ἀντίος ‘opposite’ and ἐμεῖο, the epic genitive of ἐγώ. πρὶν … παθέειν is ‘before suffering’ (epic infinitive of πάσχω). The last clause is a proverb: ῥεχθέν is the aorist passive participle of ῥέζω ‘do’, and ἔγνω is a gnomic aorist, English present.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὐ πεῖθεν· ἀμειβόμενος δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, ton d’ ou peithen· ameibomenos de prosēuda·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him he did not persuade; and answering he addressed him:
sentences.i: So he spoke, but he did not persuade him; and Panthus’ son answered and spoke to him:
sentences.n: The subject changes inside the line. In the first half Menelaus is the one speaking, and τὸν ‘him’ is Euphorbus, whom he fails to persuade; in the second half ἀμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is Euphorbus. πεῖθεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πείθω ‘persuade’. προσηύδα ‘addressed’ is imperfect of προσαυδάω. The colon introduces Euphorbus’ reply, which runs to line 42.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δὴ Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς ἦ μάλα τείσεις
γνωτὸν ἐμὸν τὸν ἔπεφνες, ἐπευχόμενος δ’ ἀγορεύεις,
sentences.tr:
nyn men dē Menelae diotrephes ē mala teiseis
gnōton emon ton epephnes, epeuchomenos d’ agoreueis,
sentences.l:
“Now indeed, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, truly you shall pay
for my kinsman whom you killed, and vaunting you speak,
sentences.i: “Now, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, you will truly pay for my kinsman whom you killed, and you talk in triumph over him,
sentences.n: The kinsman is Hyperenor, whom Menelaus killed (14.516–519) and spoke of in lines 24–28; the Greek here does not name him. γνωτός is a blood relation, and the Greek does not say which. τείσεις is the future of τίνω ‘pay (a penalty)’, with the accusative of the man for whom the price is paid. ἔπεφνες is the aorist of φένω ‘kill’, and ἐπευχόμενος is ‘vaunting’, the sense it has when it is a taunt and not a prayer. The addressee is the same Menelaus, with the stock vocative διοτρεφές, now used as a taunt.

sentences.t:
χήρωσας δὲ γυναῖκα μυχῷ θαλάμοιο νέοιο,
ἀρητὸν δὲ τοκεῦσι γόον καὶ πένθος ἔθηκας.
sentences.tr:
chērōsas de gynaika mychōi thalamoio neoio,
arēton de tokeusi goon kai penthos ethēkas.
sentences.l:
and you widowed his wife in the inner part of a new chamber,
and to his parents you made a cursed lament and grief.
sentences.i: You have widowed his wife in a new chamber, in its inner part, and brought his parents a cursed lament and grief.
sentences.n: χήρωσας is the aorist of χηρόω ‘make a widow of’. μυχῷ θαλάμοιο νέοιο is ‘in the innermost part of a new chamber’, a chamber for a newly married couple. The meaning of ἀρητόν is not certain: it is from ἀρά ‘prayer, curse’, and ‘accursed’ is the usual guess. γόον καὶ πένθος ἔθηκας is ‘you made lament and grief’ for his parents, with τοκεῦσι in the dative of interest.

sentences.t:
ἦ κέ σφιν δειλοῖσι γόου κατάπαυμα γενοίμην
εἴ κεν ἐγὼ κεφαλήν τε τεὴν καὶ τεύχε’ ἐνείκας
Πάνθῳ ἐν χείρεσσι βάλω καὶ Φρόντιδι δίῃ.
sentences.tr:
ē ke sphin deiloisi goou katapauma genoimēn
ei ken egō kephalēn te teēn kai teuche’ eneikas
Panthōi en cheiressi balō kai Phrontidi diēi.
sentences.i: I could truly become an end to the lamenting of those wretched two, if I were to bring your head and your armour and put them in the hands of Panthus and heavenly Phrontis.
sentences.n: The ‘wretched’ ones are the parents of line 37; they are now named, Panthus and Phrontis. ἦ κε … γενοίμην is a potential optative with a condition: εἴ κεν … βάλω (aorist subjunctive) is the ‘if’ clause. κατάπαυμα is ‘a means of stopping, an ending’. ἐνείκας is the aorist participle of φέρω (= ἐνέγκας) ‘having brought’. Φρόντιδι is the dative of Φρόντις; δίῃ ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ μὰν ἔτι δηρὸν ἀπείρητος πόνος ἔσται
οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἀδήριτος ἤτ’ ἀλκῆς ἤτε φόβοιο.
sentences.tr:
all’ ou man eti dēron apeirētos ponos estai
oud’ et’ adēritos ēt’ alkēs ēte phoboio.
sentences.l:
But truly no longer for long will the struggle be untried,
nor undecided, either in might or in flight.”
sentences.i: But this struggle will not be left untried for long, nor undecided, whether in might or in flight.”
sentences.n: The struggle is the duel between Menelaus and Euphorbus, which Euphorbus says will soon be settled. ἀπείρητος means ‘untried, not yet tested’ and ἀδήριτος ‘uncontested, undecided’ (from δῆρις ‘contest’), and both are used here of a πόνος ‘labour, struggle’. οὐ μάν ‘truly not’ is an emphatic negation. ἤτ’ … ἤτε is ‘either … or’. φόβοιο is the genitive of φόβος, which in Homer is ‘flight, panic’, not subjective fear.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν οὔτησε κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην·
οὐδ’ ἔρρηξεν χαλκός, ἀνεγνάμφθη δέ οἱ αἰχμὴ
ἀσπίδ’ ἐνὶ κρατερῇ·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn outēse kat’ aspida pantos’ eïsēn·
oud’ errēxen chalkos, anegnamphthē de hoi aichmē
aspid’ eni kraterēi·
sentences.i: With these words Euphorbus stabbed at the shield of Menelaus, which was equal on every side; the bronze did not break it, and its point was bent back in the strong shield;
sentences.n: Euphorbus makes the first thrust. The first line is a formula that the Iliad uses of a thrust at a shield, and the second and third lines say that the spear-point folded on the strong shield: οἱ ‘to him’ is Euphorbus, whose spear it is. οὔτησε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound, stab at’, and ἔρρηξεν the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. ἀνεγνάμφθη is the aorist passive of ἀναγνάμπτω ‘bend back’, and αἰχμή ‘point’ is the head of the spear.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ δεύτερος ὄρνυτο χαλκῷ
Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος ἐπευξάμενος Διὶ πατρί·
sentences.tr:
ho de deuteros ornyto chalkōi
Atreïdēs Menelaos epeuxamenos Dii patri·
sentences.l:
and he in second place rushed on with the bronze,
Atreus’-son Menelaus, having prayed to father Zeus;
sentences.i: and Menelaus, son of Atreus, rushed on second with the bronze, after praying to father Zeus;
sentences.n: Now it is Menelaus’ turn, after a prayer to Zeus whose words the poet does not give. ὃ δὲ is ‘and he’, with δεύτερος ‘second’ in the nominative, agreeing with the subject. ὄρνυτο is an unaugmented imperfect of ὄρνυμι (middle) ‘rush’. ἐπευξάμενος is the aorist participle of ἐπεύχομαι, here the prayer sense ‘pray to’. Ἀτρεΐδης is ‘son of Atreus’.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ἀναχαζομένοιο κατὰ στομάχοιο θέμεθλα
νύξ’, ἐπὶ δ’ αὐτὸς ἔρεισε βαρείῃ χειρὶ πιθήσας·
sentences.tr:
aps d’ anachazomenoio kata stomachoio themethla
nyx’, epi d’ autos ereise bareiēi cheiri pithēsas·
sentences.l:
and back, as he gave ground, at the foundations of the throat
he stabbed, and upon it himself pressed, trusting in his heavy hand;
sentences.i: and, as the other gave ground backward, he stabbed at the base of his throat, and pressed in on it himself, trusting in his heavy hand;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ thrust lands on Euphorbus as he gives way. ἀναχαζομένοιο is a genitive participle of ἀναχάζομαι ‘give ground back’, ‘of him giving ground back’, a second genitive that names the man whose throat it is, beside στομάχοιο θέμεθλα ‘the foundations of the throat’. νύξ’ is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’. ἔρεισε is the aorist of ἐρείδω ‘press’, and πιθήσας is the aorist participle of πείθομαι ‘trust’. Line 48 stands word for word in another duel earlier in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἁπαλοῖο δι’ αὐχένος ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκή,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
antikry d’ hapaloio di’ auchenos ēlyth’ akōkē,
doupēsen de pesōn, arabēse de teuche’ ep’ autōi.
sentences.l:
and straight through the tender neck went the point,
and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: The point went straight through his tender neck, and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: Both lines are formulas of a killing, and their English is kept from the places where they stand elsewhere. ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ is an adverb, and ἤλυθ’ is ἦλθε, the aorist of ἔρχομαι. ἀκωκή is ‘point’, as in the Odyssey’s line. δούπησεν and ἀράβησε are two verbs that make the sound: ‘fell with a thud’, and ‘clattered’. The armour is τεύχε’ (= τεύχεα), with ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘upon him’.

sentences.t:
αἵματί οἱ δεύοντο κόμαι Χαρίτεσσιν ὁμοῖαι
πλοχμοί θ’, οἳ χρυσῷ τε καὶ ἀργύρῳ ἐσφήκωντο.
sentences.tr:
haimati hoi deuonto komai Charitessin homoiai
plochmoi th’, hoi chrysōi te kai argyrōi esphēkōnto.
sentences.l:
With blood were wetted his hair, like the Graces’,
and the locks that were bound with gold and silver.
sentences.i: His hair was wet with blood, hair like the Graces’, and the locks that were bound with gold and silver.
sentences.n: The fallen man’s hair is described for its beauty: Χαρίτεσσιν ὁμοῖαι ‘like the Graces’ (Χαρίτεσσιν is the epic dative plural of Χάρις; the Charites are goddesses of charm) is a comparison of the hair. δεύοντο is the imperfect passive of δεύω ‘wet’, and αἵματι is the dative of means. πλοχμοί are ‘locks, braids’, and ἐσφήκωντο is the pluperfect passive of σφηκόω ‘bind tight’; what the gold and silver were fastened with is not said. κόμαι and πλοχμοί are the subjects of δεύοντο, and the relative οἵ (the πλοχμοί) is the subject of ἐσφήκωντο.

sentences.t:
οἷον δὲ τρέφει ἔρνος ἀνὴρ ἐριθηλὲς ἐλαίης
χώρῳ ἐν οἰοπόλῳ, ὅθ’ ἅλις ἀναβέβροχεν ὕδωρ,
καλὸν τηλεθάον·
sentences.tr:
hoion de trephei ernos anēr erithēles elaiēs
chōrōi en oiopolōi, hoth’ halis anabebrochen hydōr,
kalon tēlethaon·
sentences.i: As a man rears a flourishing shoot of olive in a lonely place where water wells up in plenty, a fair, thriving one;
sentences.n: A simile begins, and οἷον ‘as’ finds its answer in τοῖον ‘just so’ at line 59. ἔρνος is a young shoot and ἐριθηλές ‘flourishing’ is its epithet. χώρῳ ἐν οἰοπόλῳ is ‘in a lonely place’, ‘lonely’, an old guess at its sense that is not certain. ἀναβέβροχεν is a rare perfect, and its meaning is not certain: ‘has welled up’ is the usual sense. τηλεθάον ‘thriving’ is a participle of τηλεθάω.

sentences.t:
τὸ δέ τε πνοιαὶ δονέουσι
παντοίων ἀνέμων, καί τε βρύει ἄνθεϊ λευκῷ·
sentences.tr:
to de te pnoiai doneousi
pantoiōn anemōn, kai te bryei antheï leukōi·
sentences.l:
and it the breezes shake
of winds of every kind, and it teems with white blossom;
sentences.i: and the breezes of winds of every kind shake it, and it teems with white blossom;
sentences.n: Still the simile of the olive shoot. τό ‘it’ is the shoot, the object of δονέουσι ‘shake’, and πνοιαί ‘breezes’ is the subject, with παντοίων ἀνέμων ‘of winds of every kind’. δέ τε and καί τε mark a general truth, as in many similes. βρύει is ‘teems, is full of’ and takes the dative ἄνθεϊ λευκῷ ‘white blossom’.

sentences.t:
ἐλθὼν δ’ ἐξαπίνης ἄνεμος σὺν λαίλαπι πολλῇ
βόθρου τ’ ἐξέστρεψε καὶ ἐξετάνυσσ’ ἐπὶ γαίῃ·
sentences.tr:
elthōn d’ exapinēs anemos syn lailapi pollēi
bothrou t’ exestrepse kai exetanyss’ epi gaiēi·
sentences.l:
and a wind, coming suddenly with a great squall,
turns it out of its pit and stretches it out on the earth;
sentences.i: then a wind comes suddenly with a great squall, turns it out of its pit and stretches it out on the earth;
sentences.n: The simile turns: a sudden wind uproots the tree. The verbs are aorists, but a simile states what happens in general, so English uses the present. ἐλθών ‘coming’ is the aorist participle, λαῖλαψ is a ‘squall’, and βόθρου is the genitive ‘out of its pit’, the hole the tree stood in. ἐξέστρεψε is the aorist of ἐκστρέφω ‘turn out’, and ἐξετάνυσσ’ the aorist of ἐκτανύω ‘stretch out’.

sentences.t:
τοῖον Πάνθου υἱὸν ἐϋμμελίην Εὔφορβον
Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος ἐπεὶ κτάνε τεύχε’ ἐσύλα.
sentences.tr:
toion Panthou huion eÿmmeliēn Euphorbon
Atreïdēs Menelaos epei ktane teuche’ esyla.
sentences.l:
just so Panthus’ son, of the good ash-spear, Euphorbus
Atreus’-son Menelaus, when he had killed him, was stripping the armour.
sentences.i: Just so Menelaus, son of Atreus, when he had killed Euphorbus, son of Panthus, of the good ash-spear, was stripping him of his armour.
sentences.n: τοῖον answers οἷον of line 53: Euphorbus is the felled olive. The word order puts the object, Πάνθου υἱὸν ἐϋμμελίην Εὔφορβον, first and the subject Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος second. ἐπεὶ κτάνε is ‘when he had killed’ (aorist of κτείνω), and ἐσύλα is the imperfect of συλάω ‘strip’. τεύχε’ (= τεύχεα) ‘armour’ is the object of ἐσύλα.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τίς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος ἀλκὶ πεποιθὼς
βοσκομένης ἀγέλης βοῦν ἁρπάσῃ ἥ τις ἀρίστη·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote tis te leōn oresitrophos alki pepoithōs
boskomenēs agelēs boun harpasēi hē tis aristē·
sentences.l:
And as when some lion, mountain-nurtured, trusting in his might,
from a grazing herd seizes a cow, whichever is best;
sentences.i: As when a mountain-nurtured lion, trusting in his might, seizes from a grazing herd the cow that is best;
sentences.n: A new simile, for Menelaus with his prize. ὡς δ’ ὅτε τίς τε is a stock opening, ‘as when some …’. ὀρεσίτροφος ‘mountain-nurtured’ is a compound of ὄρος ‘mountain’ and τρέφω ‘nurture’, and ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς ‘trusting in his might’ is a stock phrase. βοσκομένης ἀγέλης is a genitive: ‘out of a grazing herd’. ἁρπάσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἁρπάζω ‘seize’, and ἥ τις ἀρίστη ‘whichever is best’ shows βοῦν is a cow.

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ ἐξ αὐχέν’ ἔαξε λαβὼν κρατεροῖσιν ὀδοῦσι
πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δέ θ’ αἷμα καὶ ἔγκατα πάντα λαφύσσει
δῃῶν·
sentences.tr:
tēs d’ ex auchen’ eaxe labōn krateroisin odousi
prōton, epeita de th’ haima kai enkata panta laphyssei
dēiōn·
sentences.i: First he seizes her in his strong teeth and breaks her neck, and then he gulps down the blood and all the entrails as he rends her;
sentences.n: The lion kills the cow. The first line is a formula, whose English is kept. ἔαξε is the aorist of ἄγνυμι ‘break’, in a simile where English uses the present, and λαφύσσει is ‘gulps down’. ἔγκατα are the ‘entrails’. δῃῶν is a participle of δηϊόω ‘cut down, rend’, and the lion is the subject throughout. θ’ in ἔπειτα δέ θ’ is τε, giving a general truth.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ τόν γε κύνες τ’ ἄνδρές τε νομῆες
πολλὰ μάλ’ ἰύζουσιν ἀπόπροθεν οὐδ’ ἐθέλουσιν
ἀντίον ἐλθέμεναι· μάλα γὰρ χλωρὸν δέος αἱρεῖ·
sentences.tr:
amphi de ton ge kynes t’ andres te nomēes
polla mal’ iyzousin apoprothen oud’ ethelousin
antion elthemenai· mala gar chlōron deos hairei·
sentences.i: while dogs and herdsmen raise a great cry around him from far off, and will not go against him, for pale fear takes hold of them;
sentences.n: The beast’s victory frightens those who guard the herd. τόν γε is the lion, and ἀμφί ‘around’ goes with it. ἰύζουσιν is ‘raise a cry’, of dogs and men alike, and πολλὰ μάλα makes it loud. ἐθέλουσιν … ἀντίον ἐλθέμεναι is ‘are willing to go against’ (epic infinitive), negated by οὐδ’. χλωρὸν δέος ‘pale fear’ is a stock phrase; χλωρός is the pale, greenish colour of fear.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν οὔ τινι θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐτόλμα
ἀντίον ἐλθέμεναι Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs tōn ou tini thymos eni stēthessin etolma
antion elthemenai Menelaou kydalimoio.
sentences.l:
So of them not in any one did the spirit in his chest dare
to go against glorious Menelaus.
sentences.i: So the spirit in the breast of none of them dared to go against glorious Menelaus.
sentences.n: The simile’s application: the Trojans around Menelaus are the dogs and herdsmen. τῶν is partitive, ‘of them’, with οὔ τινι ‘in no one’. ἐτόλμα is the imperfect of τολμάω ‘dare’, and θυμός is the ‘spirit’ that has the courage. κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’ is Menelaus’ epithet here, in the genitive with Μενελάου.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κε ῥεῖα φέροι κλυτὰ τεύχεα Πανθοΐδαο
Ἀτρεΐδης, εἰ μή οἱ ἀγάσσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
sentences.tr:
entha ke rheia pheroi klyta teuchea Panthoïdao
Atreïdēs, ei mē hoi agassato Phoibos Apollōn,
sentences.l:
Then easily would the son of Atreus have carried off the famous armour of Panthus’-son,
if Phoebus Apollo had not begrudged it to him,
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus would easily have carried off the famous armour of Panthus’ son, if Phoebus Apollo had not begrudged him this,
sentences.n: The poet now says what would have happened, were it not for a god. ἔνθα κε … φέροι (optative with κε) matches εἰ μή … ἀγάσσατο (aorist indicative), a past contrary-to-fact condition: ‘would have carried off, if … had not’. ἀγάσσατο is the aorist of ἄγαμαι (also ἀγάομαι) ‘begrudge, take amiss’. Πανθοΐδαο is the epic genitive of Πανθοΐδης ‘son of Panthus’, Euphorbus. κλυτά τεύχεα ‘famous armour’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥά οἱ Ἕκτορ’ ἐπῶρσε θοῷ ἀτάλαντον Ἄρηϊ
ἀνέρι εἰσάμενος Κικόνων ἡγήτορι Μέντῃ·
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hos rha hoi Hektor’ epōrse thoōi atalanton Arēï
aneri eisamenos Kikonōn hēgētori Mentēi·
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.i: who roused Hector against him, the equal of swift Ares, taking the likeness of a man, Mentes, leader of the Cicones; and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: Apollo is the god, and he rouses Hector in the likeness of a mortal, Mentes, a leader of the Cicones. ἐπῶρσε is the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rouse against’, and θοῷ ἀτάλαντον Ἄρηϊ ‘the equal of swift Ares’ is a stock phrase. εἰσάμενος is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself like’. The last line is a formula; the English of it is kept, with the pronoun changed to ‘him’ for Hector. A speech follows, in lines 75–81.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ νῦν σὺ μὲν ὧδε θέεις ἀκίχητα διώκων
ἵππους Αἰακίδαο δαΐφρονος·
sentences.tr:
Hektor nyn sy men hōde theeis akichēta diōkōn
hippous Aiakidao daïphronos·
sentences.l:
“Hector, now you thus run, pursuing the unreachable
horses of the descendant of Aeacus, the wise-minded;
sentences.i: “Hector, you are running like this, chasing the horses of the wise-hearted descendant of Aeacus, which cannot be overtaken;
sentences.n: Apollo, as Mentes, speaks to Hector. Αἰακίδαο is a patronymic, ‘descendant of Aeacus’, and it is Achilles, named in line 78; the horses are the deathless pair that carried Automedon out at the end of Book 16. ἀκίχητα is ‘not to be reached, that cannot be overtaken’; it is neuter plural beside the masculine ἵππους, so strictly it names the chase (‘pursuing the unreachable’), and both layers read it with the horses. δαΐφρονος ‘wise-hearted’ is the stock epithet, and its sense is disputed (wise or fierce). θέεις is the present of θέω ‘run’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀλεγεινοὶ
ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι δαμήμεναι ἠδ’ ὀχέεσθαι
ἄλλῳ γ’ ἢ Ἀχιλῆϊ, τὸν ἀθανάτη τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alegeinoi
andrasi ge thnētoisi damēmenai ēd’ ocheesthai
allōi g’ ē Achilēï, ton athanatē teke mētēr.
sentences.i: and they are grievous for mortal men, at least, to tame and to drive, for any but Achilles, whom an immortal mother bore.
sentences.n: These lines stand word for word elsewhere in the Iliad, and the English is kept. ἀλεγεινοί ‘grievous’ governs the infinitives δαμήμεναι ‘to be tamed’ and ὀχέεσθαι ‘to be driven’ (passive-sense epic forms), and the Greek construction is the one of ‘hard for men to tame’. ἄλλῳ γ’ ἢ Ἀχιλῆϊ is ‘for anyone other than Achilles’, and τὸν ἀθανάτη τέκε μήτηρ ‘whom an immortal mother bore’ is Achilles.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δέ τοι Μενέλαος ἀρήϊος Ἀτρέος υἱὸς
Πατρόκλῳ περιβὰς Τρώων τὸν ἄριστον ἔπεφνε
Πανθοΐδην Εὔφορβον, ἔπαυσε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.tr:
tophra de toi Menelaos arēïos Atreos huios
Patroklōi peribas Trōōn ton ariston epephne
Panthoïdēn Euphorbon, epause de thouridos alkēs.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile, Menelaus, warlike son of Atreus,
having bestridden Patroclus, killed the best of the Trojans,
Panthus’-son Euphorbus, and stopped him from impetuous might.”
sentences.i: Meanwhile Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus, standing over Patroclus, has killed the best of the Trojans, Panthus’ son Euphorbus, and made him cease from his impetuous might.”
sentences.n: τόφρα δέ τοι is ‘and meanwhile, mark you’, with τοι an ethic dative addressed to Hector. περιβάς is the aorist participle of περιβαίνω ‘bestride’ and takes the dative Πατρόκλῳ; ἔπεφνε is the aorist of φένω ‘kill’. The Trojans’ ‘best’ is a claim about Euphorbus’ rank. ἔπαυσε … θούριδος ἀλκῆς is ‘stopped from impetuous might’, a stock phrase for killing. Ἀτρέος υἱός is a periphrastic ‘son of Atreus’, and ἀρήϊος is ‘warlike’.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν αὖτις ἔβη θεὸς ἂμ πόνον ἀνδρῶν,
Ἕκτορα δ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος πύκασε φρένας ἀμφὶ μελαίνας·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn ho men autis ebē theos am ponon andrōn,
Hektora d’ ainon achos pykase phrenas amphi melainas·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he, the god, went back again into the toil of men,
but Hector a fearsome grief covered about his dark wits;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the god went back again into the toil of men, but fearsome grief covered Hector round about his dark wits;
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν … θεός is Apollo, who leaves; Ἕκτορα is the object, and the subject αἰνὸν ἄχος ‘fearsome grief’ is in the second line. ἔβη is the aorist of βαίνω. ἂμ πόνον ἀνδρῶν is ἀνὰ πόνον, ‘into the toil of men’. πύκασε is the aorist of πυκάζω ‘cover thickly’, and φρένας ‘wits’ are the seat of the mind. μελαίνας ‘dark’ is a regular epithet for φρένες.

sentences.t:
πάπτηνεν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα κατὰ στίχας, αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω
τὸν μὲν ἀπαινύμενον κλυτὰ τεύχεα, τὸν δ’ ἐπὶ γαίῃ
κείμενον· ἔρρει δ’ αἷμα κατ’ οὐταμένην ὠτειλήν.
sentences.tr:
paptēnen d’ ar’ epeita kata stichas, autika d’ egnō
ton men apainymenon klyta teuchea, ton d’ epi gaiēi
keimenon· errei d’ haima kat’ outamenēn ōteilēn.
sentences.l:
And he glanced about then along the ranks, and at once he recognised
one stripping off the famous armour, and the other upon the ground
lying; and the blood was flowing down through the stabbed wound.
sentences.i: Then he glanced along the ranks, and at once he recognised the one stripping off the famous armour and the other lying on the ground, with the blood flowing out through the wound he had been given.
sentences.n: Hector looks and sees Menelaus and the fallen Euphorbus. πάπτηνεν is the aorist of παπταίνω ‘glance about’. τὸν μέν … τὸν δ’ is ‘the one … the other’: the first is Menelaus, who is ἀπαινύμενον ‘stripping off’ the armour, and the second is Euphorbus, κείμενον ‘lying’. ἔρρει is the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’. οὐταμένην is the passive participle of οὐτάω ‘wound’, and ὠτειλή is a ‘wound’.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ
ὀξέα κεκλήγων φλογὶ εἴκελος Ἡφαίστοιο
ἀσβέστῳ·
sentences.tr:
bē de dia promachōn kekorythmenos aithopi chalkōi
oxea keklēgōn phlogi eikelos Hēphaistoio
asbestōi·
sentences.i: He went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire, with a shrill cry, like the unquenchable flame of Hephaestus;
sentences.n: Line 87 repeats line 3 of this part and stands at 5.681 and elsewhere; its English is kept. Hector charges, shouting. ὀξέα κεκλήγων is ‘shrilly shrieking’, the perfect participle of κλάζω with a present sense. φλογὶ εἴκελος is ‘like a flame’ with the dative, and Ἡφαίστοιο ‘of Hephaestus’ is the god’s name used for fire. ἀσβέστῳ ‘unquenchable’ is from σβέννυμι ‘quench’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ υἱὸν λάθεν Ἀτρέος ὀξὺ βοήσας·
ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ huion lathen Atreos oxy boēsas·
ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l:
nor did he escape the notice of the son of Atreus, shouting shrilly;
and, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And Hector did not escape the notice of the son of Atreus, as he shouted shrilly; and, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: The subject of λάθεν ‘escaped the notice of’ is Hector, and the one who hears him is Menelaus. ὀξὺ βοήσας is ‘shouting shrilly’, the aorist participle of βοάω. Line 90 is a formula for a man speaking to himself, and its English is kept. μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’ is a stock epithet of θυμός, and ὃν is the possessive ‘his own’. The colon opens Menelaus’ speech to himself, which is the rest of the part.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι ἐγὼν εἰ μέν κε λίπω κάτα τεύχεα καλὰ
Πάτροκλόν θ’, ὃς κεῖται ἐμῆς ἕνεκ’ ἐνθάδε τιμῆς,
μή τίς μοι Δαναῶν νεμεσήσεται ὅς κεν ἴδηται.
sentences.tr:
ō moi egōn ei men ke lipō kata teuchea kala
Patroklon th’, hos keitai emēs henek’ enthade timēs,
mē tis moi Danaōn nemesēsetai hos ken idētai.
sentences.l:
“Oh me, if I leave behind the fine armour
and Patroclus, who lies here for the sake of my honour,
lest some one of the Danaans feel resentment at me, whoever sees it.
sentences.i: “Oh me, if I leave behind the fine armour and Patroclus, who lies here for the sake of my honour, I fear that some Danaan will feel resentment at me, whoever sees it.
sentences.n: Menelaus is talking to his own heart, weighing two courses. The sentence breaks off: εἰ μέν κε λίπω ‘if I leave’ has no main clause, and μή τίς … νεμεσήσεται ‘lest someone feel resentment’ is a clause of fear that fills the gap, with a future indicative. κάτα … λίπω is the verb καταλείπω ‘leave behind’ split in two (tmesis). ἐμῆς ἕνεκ’ … τιμῆς is ‘for the sake of my honour’, i.e. Patroclus died in Menelaus’ cause. Δαναῶν is the genitive after τίς, and ὅς κεν ἴδηται ‘whoever sees’ is a general relative clause.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν Ἕκτορι μοῦνος ἐὼν καὶ Τρωσὶ μάχωμαι
αἰδεσθείς, μή πώς με περιστήωσ’ ἕνα πολλοί·
sentences.tr:
ei de ken Hektori mounos eōn kai Trōsi machōmai
aidestheis, mē pōs me peristēōs’ hena polloi·
sentences.l:
But if, being alone, I fight with Hector and the Trojans,
ashamed, lest somehow the many surround me, one man;
sentences.i: But if I fight Hector and the Trojans alone, out of shame, I fear that the many may somehow surround me, one man;
sentences.n: This is the second course, and again the sentence is a condition with a fear clause as its conclusion. μοῦνος ἐών is ‘being alone’, and Ἕκτορι … καὶ Τρωσί are datives after μάχωμαι ‘fight’. αἰδεσθείς is the aorist participle of αἰδέομαι, here ‘ashamed’ before the opinion of others. μή πώς με περιστήωσ’ ἕνα πολλοί is ‘lest somehow many surround me, one’, with the subjunctive aorist περιστήωσι (Attic περιστῶσι).

sentences.t:
Τρῶας δ’ ἐνθάδε πάντας ἄγει κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός;
sentences.tr:
Trōas d’ enthade pantas agei korythaiolos Hektōr.
alla ti ē moi tauta philos dielexato thymos;
sentences.l:
And all the Trojans here Hector of the glancing helmet leads.
But why indeed has my dear heart talked these things over with me?
sentences.i: Hector of the glancing helmet is leading all the Trojans here. But why has my own heart talked all this over with me?
sentences.n: The first line gives the reason for fear; Ἕκτωρ is the subject, delayed to the end with its epithet κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’. Line 97 is the formula with which a hero stops his own deliberation and turns on himself: ἦ is ‘indeed’, and φίλος θυμός is ‘my dear heart’. διελέξατο is the aorist middle of διαλέγομαι ‘talk over’, and the question is a rebuke of his own heart.

sentences.t:
ὁππότ’ ἀνὴρ ἐθέλῃ πρὸς δαίμονα φωτὶ μάχεσθαι
ὅν κε θεὸς τιμᾷ, τάχα οἱ μέγα πῆμα κυλίσθη.
sentences.tr:
hoppot’ anēr ethelēi pros daimona phōti machesthai
hon ke theos timāi, tacha hoi mega pēma kylisthē.
sentences.l:
Whenever a man is willing, against a divinity, to fight with a man
whom a god honours, soon a great woe is rolled upon him.
sentences.i: When a man is willing to fight, against a divinity, a man whom a god honours, a great woe is soon rolled upon him.
sentences.n: Menelaus states the rule that applies to Hector. ὁππότε … ἐθέλῃ is a general temporal clause with the subjunctive, and πρὸς δαίμονα ‘against a divinity’ is the thing opposed. The man fought is φωτί ‘a man’, ὅν κε … τιμᾷ ‘whomever a god honours’ (a general relative clause with the subjunctive). κυλίσθη is the aorist passive of κυλίνδω ‘roll’, unaugmented (ἐκυλίσθη) and gnomic, in a general statement: the woe is rolled upon (οἱ) the aggressor. τάχα ‘soon’ and πῆμα ‘woe’ are the plain words.

sentences.t:
τώ μ’ οὔ τις Δαναῶν νεμεσήσεται ὅς κεν ἴδηται
Ἕκτορι χωρήσαντ’, ἐπεὶ ἐκ θεόφιν πολεμίζει.
sentences.tr:
tō m’ ou tis Danaōn nemesēsetai hos ken idētai
Hektori chōrēsant’, epei ek theophin polemizei.
sentences.l:
Therefore no one of the Danaans will feel resentment at me, whoever sees me
yielding to Hector, since he fights from gods.
sentences.i: So none of the Danaans who sees me give way to Hector will feel resentment at me, since he fights with divine help.
sentences.n: τώ ‘so, therefore’ draws the conclusion. Line 100 repeats the end of line 93, with οὔ in place of μή: he now says the Danaans will not blame him. χωρήσαντ’ is χωρήσαντα, an aorist participle agreeing with the unspoken ‘me’ (‘me having given way’), and Ἕκτορι is the dative ‘to Hector’. ἐκ θεόφιν has the old ending -φιν and does not mark the number, so it is ‘from god(s)’; the sense is that Hector fights with a god’s help, and Apollo has just roused him.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ που Αἴαντός γε βοὴν ἀγαθοῖο πυθοίμην,
ἄμφω κ’ αὖτις ἰόντες ἐπιμνησαίμεθα χάρμης
καὶ πρὸς δαίμονά περ, εἴ πως ἐρυσαίμεθα νεκρὸν
Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ·
sentences.tr:
ei de pou Aiantos ge boēn agathoio pythoimēn,
amphō k’ autis iontes epimnēsaimetha charmēs
kai pros daimona per, ei pōs erysaimetha nekron
Pēleïdēi Achilēï·
sentences.l:
But if somewhere I might hear of Ajax, good at the war-cry,
both of us, going again, might be mindful of the joy of battle,
even against a divinity, if somehow we might drag the corpse
for Peleus’-son Achilles;
sentences.i: But if I could somewhere hear of Ajax, good at the war-cry, we two could go back and bring to mind the joy of battle, even against a divinity, if somehow we might drag the corpse away for Achilles, son of Peleus;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ third thought: find Ajax. εἰ … πυθοίμην is the ‘if’ clause of a remote condition (‘if I could hear of’), with Αἴαντος in the genitive, and βοὴν ἀγαθοῖο ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet in the genitive. ἄμφω κ’ … ἐπιμνησαίμεθα is its conclusion, a potential optative; ἐπιμνησαίμεθα takes the genitive χάρμης ‘the joy of battle’, so ‘be mindful of’. πρὸς δαίμονά περ ‘even against a divinity’ takes up line 98, and ἐρυσαίμεθα is the aorist optative of ἐρύω ‘drag’. Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ is a dative of interest, ‘for Achilles’.

sentences.t: κακῶν δέ κε φέρτατον εἴη.
sentences.tr: kakōn de ke phertaton eiē.
sentences.l: and of evils it would be the best.”
sentences.i: and it would be the best of evils.”
sentences.n: κακῶν δέ κε φέρτατον εἴη is ‘and it would be the best of evils’, a potential optative: if the body can be got to Achilles, that is the best that can be had among evils. φέρτατον is the superlative of φέρτερος and means ‘best’ here, not ‘strongest’. The speech closes here, where the edition prints a full stop.
